title: Module quiz: How a language model works, for engineers

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A team runs two assistants on Claude Sonnet 5.5: one drafts campaign slogans and the other reads amounts off bills. The lead wants the slogans varied and the amounts exact, and plans to tune each assistant's randomness separately through request settings. What actually happens?

options.text: Anything but the defaults comes back as a 400 error, so correctness has to be enforced by checks in code
options.says: Claude Sonnet 5.5, like Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, rejects any non-default temperature, top_p or top_k with an error, so exactness for the bills comes from restricting and validating the output, and the slogans need no extra setting (the sampling section).

options.text: Each assistant takes its own value, so slogan variety and amount accuracy can be tuned independently
options.says: Ruled out because the Messages reference says "all other values will be rejected", so no assistant can take a value of its own.

options.text: Zero is accepted for the amounts assistant and then makes every output come out identical
options.says: Ruled out because even where a zero is accepted, "even with temperature set to 0, the results will not be fully deterministic", and these models reject it.

options.text: Only top_p stays adjustable, so slogans can still be varied through that one setting
options.says: Ruled out because the migration guide names all three parameters: "Omit temperature, top_p, and top_k, or leave them at their defaults: any other value is rejected".

origin.section: What the current models let you set

questions.stem: A team plans to cut wrong answers by running every prompt three times and comparing the replies. It budgets the cost from what a token-counting tool reported for Claude Haiku 4.5. After the job moves to Claude Opus 5.5 the bill is about a third above budget, although the run count is as planned. Which earlier step would have given a sound budget?

options.text: Reusing the Haiku numbers, since Claude generations share one tokenizer
options.says: Ruled out because "Tokenizers change between model generations", so the old numbers do not carry over.

options.text: Dropping the comparison runs, since every extra run is another paid request
options.says: Ruled out because the run count was already budgeted and the bill still rose: "the same text produces about 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models", so the cost moved with the model and not with the runs.

options.text: Querying the endpoint again with the destination model named, before the change
options.says: The token counting endpoint returns an estimate against the model you name, and the same text yields about 30 percent more tokens from Opus 4.7 on, so a count made for the model the job moves to would have shown the rise (page 1, tokens are not words).

options.text: Setting max_tokens low, so output cost cannot exceed the plan
options.says: Ruled out because "max_tokens is a cap on output, not on context", and the input side is where the new tokenizer adds tokens.

questions.stem: A scheduling assistant is asked to book "next Friday" mid-conversation and proposes a day from its training period. Which fix sits at the right layer?

options.text: Switch to the newest model, whose cutoff is closest to today
options.says: Ruled out because "Knowledge comes from training data with a cut-off", so even the newest model stops before today.

options.text: Have the application put the current calendar date in every request
options.says: The model has no clock, so the date has to be supplied in the context on every call (the knowledge section).

options.text: Add a prompt line telling it never to guess the current day
options.says: Ruled out because a prompt shapes the distribution and that is "why it is only a request", so a line cannot supply a fact the model lacks.

options.text: Resend older conversations with each call so they hint at today's date
options.says: Ruled out because "The model has no clock", so replaying older conversations gives it nothing to read the present from.

origin.section: What the model knows, and when it stopped knowing

questions.stem: A long contract is pasted into a request. The overview Claude returns cites a clause number that does not appear in the contract. Which prompt change most directly targets this failure?

options.text: Ask for a longer, more detailed summary so every clause is covered
options.says: Ruled out because "a plausible-looking fact is a likely continuation whether or not it is true", so more output only gives an invented clause more chances to appear.

options.text: Ask Claude to state its confidence level beside each citation
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "confidence is not evidence".

options.text: Tell it to be an honest assistant that cites only clauses that really exist in the text
options.says: Ruled out because honesty is "a goal of training and not a guarantee of any single answer", so asking for it does not ground the citations.

options.text: Have it first copy the relevant passages out exactly, then write only from them
options.says: Grounding the work in exact passages first means every claim can be traced to text that exists, which is the documented technique for long documents (the hallucination list).
